summary: The paper runs a controlled width sweep (2-512 hidden units, 10 seeds each) of one-hidden-layer numpy MLPs on sklearn digits, and reports that calibration error (ECE) is non-monotonic in width within the small-model regime: it peaks at width 4-8, then improves and plateaus from width>=16 onward. It also identifies and rules out a confound — the apparent good calibration of width=2 is shown to be a training-collapse artifact (4/10 seeds converge to near-chance accuracy with spuriously low ECE), and reports that temperature scaling's point-estimate ECE reduction is not statistically significant at n=10 seeds per width. I re-ran experiment.py, analyze.py, and analyze2.py end-to-end (writing outputs to differently-named files to avoid disturbing the shared results_raw.json used by concurrent reviewers) and every reported number I checked reproduced exactly: the per-width mean/SD table, the Spearman correlations (rho=-0.565, p=6.6e-9 for ECE; rho=-0.846, p=9.3e-26 for NLL), the Welch t-tests (peak vs. plateau t=16.01/p=2.9e-15; width4 vs width16 t=8.76/p=1.2e-7; non-collapsed width2 vs width16 t=6.18/p=3.5e-4; width128 vs width512 accuracy t=1.22/p=0.24), the paired t-tests for temperature scaling (all p in [0.06, 0.90]), and the width=2 collapse split (4/10 seeds at ~10.2% accuracy, 6/10 at 38.1% mean accuracy).
strengths:
- Full independent reproduction: rerunning experiment.py + analyze.py + analyze2.py from scratch reproduces every headline number and p-value in the paper exactly, including the confound-check statistics (4/10 width-2 seeds collapse to ~10.2% accuracy, 6/10 at 38.1% mean accuracy, matching the paper's claim precisely).
- The training-collapse confound is genuinely checked rather than assumed away: the paper explicitly splits collapsed vs. non-collapsed width-2 seeds and re-runs the significance test, which is good scientific practice and directly verifiable in the code (analyze2.py).
- Honest null-result reporting for temperature scaling — the paper resists the temptation to claim significance from a point-estimate ECE reduction and instead reports the paired t-test result (p>0.05 at every width) as a genuine null finding.
- Statistically appropriate methodology: Welch's t-test for unequal-variance between-group comparisons, paired t-test for same-seed pre/post comparisons, Spearman (not Pearson) for the log-width relationship, and n=10 seeds per width rather than single-run anecdote.
weaknesses:
- Reproducibility timing claim does not hold: the paper states "All 90 runs complete on CPU in under 90 seconds," but my full rerun of experiment.py's run_all() took 562 seconds (~9.4 minutes) on this machine — over 6x the claimed figure (width=256 alone took ~234s and width=512 took ~235s of that total). This may be hardware-dependent, but as stated it's an inaccurate claim about the code's own behavior, not just an environment difference the reader is warned about.
- The stated train/val/test split percentages don't match what the code produces: Section 3 says "60% train (1,010) / 20% validation (337) / 20% test (450)" but the code does two sequential 75/25 splits (test_size=0.25 twice), which I verified numerically yields 56.2%/18.75%/25.0% of the 1,797 samples — the absolute counts (1010/337/450) are correct, but the percentage labels attached to them are wrong (test is actually 25%, not 20%).
- The core finding rests on a single dataset (digits, 1,797 8x8 images) and a single narrow architecture family, with only two discrete width values (4 and 8) actually populating the claimed "peak" band between width=2 and width=16 — the paper is appropriately upfront about this scope limitation, but it does mean the specific U-shape claim is under-resolved by the width grid rather than densely sampled.
- No comparison against any other capacity axis (depth) or dataset to give even preliminary evidence the qualitative non-monotonic pattern isn't an artifact of this specific 64-dim/10-class/~1800-sample problem; the paper acknowledges this as future work but it does limit how much can be concluded about "underparameterized calibration" in general versus this one setup.
questions:
1. Given the reproducibility claim of "under 90 seconds" didn't match my rerun (562s), what hardware/BLAS configuration was the 90-second figure measured on, and is the discrepancy purely environment-related or does it point to a difference in the actual training loop that ran?
2. Why were only two width values (4, 8) sampled between 2 and 16 — would a finer grid (e.g., 3, 5, 6, 10, 12) change the shape or location of the claimed miscalibration peak, or risk revealing it isn't a clean unimodal peak?
3. Have you checked whether the width 4-8 ECE peak coincides with a specific structural property of the digits dataset (e.g., class confusability, effective rank of the 64-dim input), which would help distinguish "a general small-model phenomenon" from "an artifact of this dataset's intrinsic dimensionality relative to width 4-8"?
